instructions: See docs/ratings.md. Give every season a rating on the absolute scale. Rate the player that season, never their career.

seasons.note: Germany’s first choice and an ever-present in an unbeaten side; elite, a rung below the very best keepers.
Ten clean sheets across a Champions League run at thirty-five; his best Arsenal season after the first.
Lost the shirt to Almunia and did not get it back.
PFA Team of the Year after a broken leg cost him most of 1995/96; eight assists from left-back and the best left-foot delivery in the division that season.
Two divisions and two seasons on from Liverpool; at 31 a steady, well-delivered left-back for a newly promoted side rather than the PFA pick of 1996/97.
Thirty-six starts and Chelsea’s player of the year in a side that took a Champions League place on the last day; for two seasons among the best three or four keepers in the division.
Thirty-three and the best player in a mid-table Spurs side; the late runs and the finishing were intact, the legs less so.
A January arrival who took half a season to adjust; rated as the player of those months, not the one he became.
A European Cup and the PFA side; among the best left backs in the world by now.
Thirty-four and a Juventus regular; still an excellent full back, plainly past the United peak.
Eleven assists and an England cap; elite delivery, nothing else above the standard.
Two seasons outside the top flight in between; at 34 a squad left-sided player whose delivery was still the only part of his game above the level.
Two lost seasons at Leeds and abroad in between; at 28 a fringe player for a promoted side, not the England winger of 1994.
Six starts for a Bradford side relegated with 26 points; at 29 he was finished as a top-flight footballer.
Six years of Rangers, PSV and knee trouble between this and the Everton rows; he came back a lesser player.
Eleven assists from wide after two seasons out of the side; Wimbledon’s set-piece taker.
Ever-present captain of a promoted Portsmouth side that stayed up; a better defender at 33 than he had been at Barnsley six years earlier.
Arguably the best goalkeeper outside the top four in this season; shot-stopping close to elite, sits with Flowers (81) rather than Seaman (86).
Half a season of the best form of his career before a January move to Real Madrid; aggressive, a better passer than the caricature, and Everton’s driving force in a fourth-placed side.
The same season and the same footballer as the Everton row; the move did not change him.
Eighteen goals at twenty-one; a finisher of genuine top-flight quality with very little else in the game.
Twenty-four goals for a mid-table side and an England place; the best version of a narrow player.
The attacking left-back of the side that led the title race by twelve points; genuinely good going forward, regularly exposed defending.
Thirty-one and losing his place; fifteen starts in his last regular top-flight season.
Thirty-three, thirty-seven starts, and a centre-half in a Bolton side that finished sixth; durable and well organised, never quick.
Thirty-five and a third-choice keeper covering three games; still competent, well short of the Newcastle regular of the mid-1990s.
His one season as a first-choice centre-half in a title-winning side; a good defender rather than the liability he is remembered as.
Half a season in each division after a January move; one player, one number.
Half a season in each division after a January move; one player, one number.
Young Player of the Year the season before and a better footballer in this one; the beating of a full back either way.
Ten starts for a Leicester side relegated with 28 points; two seasons on from Derby and past his best.
Twenty-seven and reduced to ten starts by the knee and back problems that ended his career two years later.
A back injury ended his career at 28; five starts and no real football after them.
Three years on from the Tottenham rows; thirty-three starts in a cup-final side and the best form of his career.
Five years and two divisions on from Newcastle; a promoted Fulham’s squad midfielder at 28, still a tidy passer and nothing more.
The last full season before the illness that ended his career at 31; still a competent Premier League centre-half here.
Ruptured cruciate ligament in the third game; he never played regular top-flight football again.
A season on from the cruciate rupture and visibly not the player of 1998/99; twelve starts, and then out of the top flight for good.
Arrived from Major League Soccer in January and was immediately Blackburn’s best defender: strong, brave and a genuinely good organiser.
A genuine Premier League left-back - fit, sound defensively, limited going forward.
A title-winning centre-forward in his first English season: physically overwhelming and a real creator with his back to goal, but the finishing and decision-making were years from the player of 2009.
Twenty league goals and the Golden Boot; the season the hold-up play and the finishing arrived together.
A knee problem cost him most of the season; a dip in availability rather than in ability.
Twenty-nine goals, a second Golden Boot and the double; world class by any reading.
Fifteen goals and eight assists at 22; strong, aggressive and a better footballer than the caricature. His peak season.
Twelve starts and six goals for a relegated Coventry before his knee gave out; the physical game was already blunted.
Eighteen, already quick and positionally sound enough for Wenger to use in a title season, but a long way from the France international he became.
Thirty-seven starts and the PFA team of the year at twenty-two.
On loan from Lyon at 21 and visibly a good footballer for his size; rated as the raw version, not the Sevilla forward.
Eleven league goals from 27 starts; unusually mobile and technical for a forward of his size, and West Ham’s best attacker that season.
Higher at thirty-one than at twenty-six, which is unusual and here deliberate: he was a substantially better centre forward at Sevilla than in England, and African Footballer of the Year in between.
The right-sided supply line for the Quinn/Phillips partnership; the delivery was essentially the whole game.
Twenty-two goals for a promoted side that finished third; pace, power, finishing and genuine creation.
The decline from here is real and well documented — depression, loss of form, loss of the physical edge — rather than a run of bad luck.
Five starts, then retirement at 29; the athleticism and confidence that made him an 85 in 1995/96 were gone entirely.
